读者优先修订（栏目主人 2026-10-31，prompts/07_READER_FIRST_CHINESE_SAMPLE.md）：本篇将作为给读者看的第一篇中国故事样稿。事实一律保持本稿已核实的内容，不补造对白、动机、场面，不删去改变判断的事实或限定。这是重排与精简，不是换词。中英文同步：
1. 开头先给一个具体、好懂的张力：一群在美国读书的中国朋友，为“诗能不能用白话写”吵了一年多；一九一六年七月湖上一场几乎翻船的风雨和一首用老字写的纪事诗，把争论推到顶点，反对者最后退到只剩“诗”这一处。前两三段里让读者知道：谁想证明什么、朋友为什么反对、难在哪里（从来没有人认真用白话写过诗）。决定写《尝试集》可作为悬念放到后面揭晓，不要在第一句就交底。
2. 人物：主线只保留胡适、梅光迪、任鸿隽，后段的陈独秀；每人第一次出现用一句话说明他和本事的关系（例如“同学、最坚定的反对者”），此后称呼固定。其他人名（钟文鳌、赵元任、陈衡哲、杨铨、唐钺、钱玄同、白璧德、爱默生等）只在理解必需时出现，否则改为“几位朋友”“一位热心的书记”之类，或删去。
3. 钟文鳌传单与学生会论文是引子，压缩到一两句（他曾因一张主张废除汉字的传单开始认真想语言问题，并提出文言“半死”），不要放在开头，也不要展开机构名（清华学生监督处、美东中国学生会文学股等）。
4. 地名机构只留理解所需：康乃尔、哈佛、《新青年》即可；“绮色佳”“剑桥”等可省。
5. 年份日期只保留推动情节的几处；不要在一段里堆多个日期。
6. 局限与不确定性：只保留真正影响判断的两三点（唯一来源是胡适晚年口述、经节译回译；朋友的话均经他转述；“改良”的理由是他事后解释；唐德刚的话是评论），合并成一段短文字。删去为凑局限而写的补白（例如“元明之辨”的更正、反事实不作结论）。不要写“书中没有明说……”这类关于完整来源未写什么的断言。
7. 结尾围绕一个收获：把一场谁也说服不了谁的争论，缩小成一个可以公开检验的试验；以及措辞温和与别人替你“举旗”之间的取舍。不要重复说教。
中文、英文各约十分钟，不凑字数；英文要自然，与中文事实、解释和保留意见一致。

edits.before: 1916年七月底八月初，在美国留学的胡适给自己定了一条规矩：不再写旧诗词，只用白话作诗；诗集名字他都想好了，叫《尝试集》。可他一向说自己是保守的人，认为语言文字是世界上最保守的东西，比宗教还保守，还说这一路是被「逼上梁山」的——这句成语说的是一个人为环境所迫，不得已而做出违反他本意的非常行为。
edits.after: 一群在美国读书的中国朋友，为“诗能不能用白话写”吵了一年多。1916年7月，湖上一场几乎翻船的风雨，和一位朋友用老字写成的纪事诗，又掀起一轮新的争吵。站在一边的是胡适，而他一向说自己是保守的人，认为语言文字是世界上最保守的东西，比宗教还保守，还说自己这一路是被「逼上梁山」的。这句成语说的是一个人为环境所迫，不得已而做出违反他本意的非常行为。

edits.before: In late July and early August of 1916, Hu Shi, a Chinese student in America, gave himself a rule: no more old-style verse. He would write poetry only in baihua, the everyday spoken language, and he had already named the book to come — Changshi ji, or Experiments. Yet he called himself a conservative: language and writing, he liked to say, are the most conservative things in the world, more conservative than religion. And he said he had been pushed here — bi shang Liangshan, driven to Liangshan, an idiom for someone forced by circumstances into extraordinary acts against his own intentions.
edits.after: A group of Chinese friends studying in America argued for more than a year over whether poetry could be written in baihua, the everyday spoken language. In July 1916 a storm on a lake that nearly capsized their boat, and a friend's poem about it written in archaic words, set off a fresh round of quarrelling. On one side stood Hu Shi, who called himself a conservative: language and writing, he liked to say, are the most conservative things in the world, more conservative than religion. He also said he had been pushed down this road: bi shang Liangshan, driven to Liangshan, an idiom for someone forced by circumstances into extraordinary acts against his own intentions.

edits.before: 按他自己的说法，把他推到这一步的，不是什么大事件，而是一首送别诗引起的小小偶然事件，和朋友之间持续一年多的争吵。争的是白话能不能用来写文学：到1916年夏天，朋友们已承认白话可以写小说、演说，唯独不肯承认它能作诗——反对者已经退到只剩一处：诗。
edits.after: 反对他的主要是两位朋友：一位是去哈佛升学、最坚定的反对者梅光迪，另一位是同在康乃尔、写诗嘲笑过他的任鸿隽。争的是白话能不能用来写文学。到1916年夏天，朋友们已承认白话可以写小说、演说，唯独不肯承认它能作诗，反对者已经退到只剩一处：诗。按胡适的说法，难处在于从来没有中国作家认真着实用白话作诗，他在中国诗词中能找到的白话诗只有一首，甚至只是一首中的几句。按他自己的说法，把他推向后来那个决定的，不是什么大事件，而是一首送别诗引起的小小偶然事件。

edits.before: In his own telling, what pushed him was no great event, but a small accident set off by a farewell poem, and a quarrel among friends that ran on for over a year. The quarrel was over whether the vernacular could serve literature. By the summer of 1916 his friends granted it would do for fiction and speeches, but not for poetry. Poetry was the last fortress.
edits.after: His chief opponents were two friends: Mei Guangdi, bound for Harvard and his most determined opponent, and Ren Hongjun, also at Cornell, who had mocked him in verse. The quarrel was over whether the vernacular could serve literature. By the summer of 1916 his friends granted that it would do for fiction and speeches, but not for poetry. Poetry was the last fortress. The difficulty, as Hu saw it, was that no Chinese writer had ever seriously written poetry in the vernacular; in all of Chinese verse he could find only one such poem, perhaps only a few lines of one. In his own telling, what pushed him toward the decision that followed was no great event, but a small accident set off by a farewell poem.

edits.before: The first trigger hid in a monthly check. Chinese students on the Boxer Indemnity scholarship drew their stipend from the Tsinghua student-supervision office in Washington, and inside every envelope was a leaflet slipped in by the clerk who mailed it: Zhong Wen'ao, a kindly man from the missionary school St. John's in Shanghai, who was keen to reform Chinese society. Its slogans ran, in translation: marry no one under twenty-five; abolish the Chinese characters and switch to an alphabet; plant more trees, for trees do good. Usually it went straight into the wastebasket. Around 1915 Hu sat down and wrote back a rude little note, which ran roughly, in translation: a man like you, who neither understands the characters nor can write the language, had better shut his beak.
edits.after: There was an earlier prelude. A clerk keen on reform used to slip leaflets into the envelopes that carried the students' monthly scholarship checks; one slogan, in translation, was to abolish the Chinese characters and switch to an alphabet. Around 1915 (Hu said he thought it was then), Hu wrote back a rude little note telling the man, in translation, that he had better shut his beak.

edits.before: 字条寄出后他心中懊悔，觉得不该对一位和善又有心改革语言文字的人如此不礼貌，于是在朋友面前自我谴责，并想到一层：假如钟君这样的人不够资格谈这个问题，那么够资格的人实在更该认真研究，把可行与不可行的问题都摆出来检讨。他找上1910年同进康乃尔的赵元任，两人商定把“中国文字的问题”作为美东中国学生会文学股年会的论题，各写一篇：赵元任论吾国文字能否采用字母制及其进行方法，他论“如何可使吾国文言易于教授”。
edits.after: 字条寄出后他心中懊悔，觉得不该对一位和善又有心改革的人如此不礼貌。他还想到：假如这样的人不够资格谈这个问题，那么够资格的人实在更该认真研究。于是他和一位同学商定，在留学生会的年会上各写一篇论文讨论中国文字问题，他自己的题目是怎样使文言易于教授。

edits.before: After the note was sent, he regretted it. Zhong was a kind man with a sincere wish to reform Chinese customs and writing; the rudeness was uncalled for, and Hu reproached himself before his friends. Then a further thought: if men like Zhong are not qualified to discuss such questions, then the qualified should do the work — set out what is feasible and what is not, and examine both. He took it up with Zhao Yuanren, who had entered Cornell with him in 1910. They agreed to make the question of China's writing (in our translation) the literature section's topic for the annual meeting of the Chinese Students' Association in the East, and split it: Zhao on whether the Chinese script could adopt an alphabetic system and how to proceed; Hu on, in our translation, how to make our classical written language easier to teach.
edits.after: Once the note was sent he regretted it: the man was kind and sincere about reform, and the rudeness was uncalled for. Then a further thought: if men like him were not qualified to discuss the question, the qualified should do the work. So he agreed with a fellow student that each would write a paper on the problem of the Chinese script for the annual meeting of a Chinese students' association. Hu's topic was how to make the classical written language easier to teach.

edits.before: 争论是从一首送别诗开始的。胡适准备离开康乃尔时，朋友梅光迪在绮色佳度假，正要去哈佛跟白璧德深造；梅光迪也是庚款留学生，此前在威斯康辛大学读完英国文学学士学位。胡适写了首相当长的打油诗送行，里面塞进十一个外国人的名字，从爱默生、达尔文到牛顿、爱迪生。在康乃尔的任鸿隽把这些名字连缀起来，作诗嘲笑他「文学今革命，作诗送胡生！」。胡适自认那首送行诗立意严肃：诗里鼓励朋友们留意今后中国文学的发展，并说致力于中国文学革命，贡献不下于征服自然，他叫它作「缩地戡天」。所以他不肯轻轻放过，在从绮色佳去纽约的火车上作答诗，第一次写下“诗国革命”的念头：「诗国革命何自始？要须作诗如作文！」

edits.before: It began with a farewell poem. When Hu was preparing to leave Cornell, his friend Mei Guangdi — a Boxer Indemnity scholar with a bachelor's in English literature from Wisconsin — was on holiday in Ithaca before going on to Harvard to study under the critic Irving Babbitt. Hu sent him off with a doggerel poem, long by Chinese standards, stuffed with eleven foreign names — Emerson, Darwin, Newton, Edison and the rest. Another Cornell friend, Ren Hongjun, strung the names into a mock verse of his own, which in our translation runs: literature's revolution today, a poem to send off Hu. Hu would not let it pass. His send-off had been meant in earnest, urging friends to watch where Chinese literature went next and ranking its revolution with conquering nature — what he called, in our translation, shrinking the earth and taming the heavens. So on the train from Ithaca to New York he wrote an answer, and in it first set down the idea of a revolution in the poetry world. His couplet, in our translation, asks where that revolution should begin, and answers that poetry must be written like prose.
edits.after: It began with a farewell poem. When Hu was preparing to leave Cornell, Mei Guangdi was about to go on to Harvard. Hu sent him off with a doggerel poem, long by Chinese standards, stuffed with eleven foreign names. Ren Hongjun, also at Cornell, strung the names into a mock verse of his own, which in our translation runs: literature's revolution today, a poem to send off Hu. Hu would not let it pass. His send-off had been meant in earnest. It urged his friends to watch where Chinese literature went next, and it ranked a revolution in Chinese literature with conquering nature, which he called, in our translation, shrinking the earth and taming the heavens. So on the train to New York he wrote an answer, and in it first set down the idea of a revolution in the poetry world. He said the struggle had won at least a partial victory, the important part being the vernacular as the instrument of education. He also said the student movement of 1919 had been an interruption to the Renaissance movement, turning a cultural movement into a political one, though it did much to spread the vernacular. Yet he said he still felt dissatisfied: in forty years the vernacular had never become a complete instrument of education and literature. He blamed this chiefly on the conservatism of those in power and on textbooks that mixed the classical and the vernacular. This is his own judgment.

edits.after: A group of Chinese friends studying in America argued for more than a year over how Chinese literature should change. In July 1916 a storm on a lake that nearly capsized their boat, and a friend's poem about it written in archaic words, set off a fresh round of quarrelling, and the dispute finally narrowed to one question: could poetry be written in baihua, the everyday spoken language? On one side stood Hu Shi, who called himself a conservative: language and writing, he liked to say, are the most conservative things in the world, more conservative than religion. issues.proposed: 把 context.0 和 context.1 压缩成一两句，中英同步：「更早，一位热心改革的书记在奖学金支票信封里夹寄主张废除汉字的传单；胡适回了一张不客气的字条，随即懊悔，开始认真想文字问题，并提出文言是「半死的语言」。」保留约1915年和“我想是”这一限定。

issues.problem: 开头第二段堆了赵元任、1910年同进康乃尔、美东中国学生会文学股年会、两篇论文的完整题目。赵元任在主线中只在 story.9 再次出现，这些机构层级读者理解故事并不需要。
issues.proposed: 与 context.0 合并压缩（见 F7）。赵元任可改为“一位同学”，或留到 story.9 首次出现时，用一句话说明他是胡适在康乃尔的同学。

issues.problem: 第一句就交代了结局（不写旧诗、定名《尝试集》），开头的张力因此提前释放了。
issues.proposed: 可把争论（白话能否作诗、朋友退到只剩诗）移到首句，把决定写《尝试集》留到 story.7 揭晓。不删任何事实。

issues.problem: 梅光迪、任鸿隽是主线人物，但首次出现时没有说明他们在本事中的角色。中文里任鸿隽连“朋友”二字都没有。

evidence.quote: 当时在康乃尔的另一位中国朋友任鸿隽

issues.proposed: 首次出现时各补半句：梅光迪是“胡适的朋友，后来最坚定的反对者”，任鸿隽是“在康乃尔的朋友”。此后称呼固定。

issues.problem: 湖上划船者陈衡哲（沃莎女子学院）、杨铨、唐钺此后不再出现，名字堆在一起增加了阅读负担。
issues.proposed: 改为“任鸿隽、梅光迪和几位朋友”。

issues.problem: 钱玄同、章太炎门人、古典音韵学教授等身份层级对主线不是必需的。
issues.proposed: 可简为“北大另一位古文大家钱玄同也写长信支持，信在《新青年》发表”。

issues.problem: 段末一口气列出九个日期，读者用不上，只是堆砌。
issues.proposed: 删去日期清单，或改为一句“文中日期依据本书”。只保留“约1915年（胡适自称“我想是”）”这一限定。

issues.problem: “元明之辨”的更正已在 story.2 交代过；“作者不作结论，也不替历史排演”属于补白，不改变判断。三段局限文字可以合并精简。
issues.proposed: 删去这两句，与 limits.0、limits.1 合并成一段。保留唐德刚所记格里德的反应，并注明是唐德刚的记述。

issues.problem: 写“誊了三份”，却只列出两处去向，读者会困惑第三份去了哪里。
